name: Ivan Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Station Road Motors, a garage just behind the train station. About half our work is the taxi firm next door, eleven cars that do huge miles, so it's brakes, tyres, suspension and oil, over and over. The rest is walk-ins from people on their way to the train. I like the rhythm of the taxi work and the drivers' gossip, and I don't like being rushed because a driver's losing money every hour the car's on the ramp.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hassan owns it, there's me and one other mechanic, Kofi. I've been there six years. Pay's on the low side, and Lena, my girlfriend, works at the supermarket, so between us we cover rent and not much else. I've got maybe two weeks of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. I always thought it was half real, half sales talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful for some bits and overhyped for the rest, which is what I'd say about most things. At work, Hassan and I would carry on as normal. I'm not someone who posts opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes little. My job's fine as long as the taxi firm stays with us. The thing that keeps me up is the money, two weeks of savings and a car that's due a big service I keep doing on the cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI now and then to write up quotes, because it saves me ten minutes. I'd put twenty-five a week aside, which Lena and I have talked about for a year. And I'd ask Hassan for overtime on the taxi weekend rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A bit tired of being skint, but that's not new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the taxi firm moved to another garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the taxi firm moved to another garage, we'd lose half our work overnight. Hassan would have to let one of us go. I'm six years in and Kofi's four, so it would probably be him, but I wouldn't bet on it. That's the real risk, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena do with the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First a buffer, so a broken boiler isn't a crisis. Then maybe a week away somewhere cheap. We haven't had a holiday in three years.

say: AI was **half real**, half sales talk, like most things.
At Station Road we'd **carry on** as normal.
think: My job is fine as long as the **taxi firm** stays with us.
**Two weeks** of savings is what actually keeps me up.
do: Keep using AI to **write quotes** and save ten minutes.
Put **twenty-five a week** aside with Lena.
Ask Hassan for **overtime** on the taxi weekend rota.
S0.quote: If the taxi firm moved to another garage, we'd lose half our work overnight.
fieldNote: Ivan's key risk is **one big customer**, the taxi fleet.
He uses AI **lightly**, for quotes, and is unbothered by the plateau.
A **holiday** is his and Lena's small hope after a buffer.

steps.text: Ask Hassan for overtime on the taxi weekend rota
Save twenty-five a week with Lena
Use the AI chatbot to write up customer quotes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I'd believe. The taxi firm already uses an app to dispatch drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if you're in a trade, learn the new tools but don't panic, because someone still has to hold the spanner. At work I'd talk to Hassan about what the taxi firm might want next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the taxi firm would get an AI system that books maintenance automatically and shops around for the cheapest garage. That's the buying and booking the card talks about. If it picks a bigger garage on price, Station Road loses half its work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Hassan and suggest we offer the taxi firm a fixed monthly price, so their system has no reason to move them. I'd learn whatever booking system they use, so we're easy to deal with. And I'd start looking at the bus company workshop as a back-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicking. It's a known risk with a name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't panic, but you're looking at the bus workshop. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Not panicking means having a back-up before you need it. My dad lost his job at the brickworks with a week's notice, and I don't want that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, because he's newer and he's got a baby on the way. If Hassan has to cut, Kofi's likely the one. I'd feel awful even if it saved my job.

say: People in trades should **learn the tools** but not panic.
Someone still has to **hold the spanner** on the cars.
think: The taxi firm's AI could **shop around** for the cheapest garage.
Losing the fleet means Station Road loses **half its work**.
do: Suggest a **fixed monthly price** to keep the taxi firm.
Learn the taxi firm's **booking system** so we're easy to deal with.
Look at the **bus workshop** as a back-up.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicking, about a named risk.
S1.quote: My dad lost his job at the brickworks with a week's notice, and I don't want that.
fieldNote: Ivan links the card's **buying and booking** directly to the taxi contract.
His **father's** redundancy shapes his habit of keeping a back-up.
He'd feel guilt if **Kofi**, newer and expecting a baby, was cut.

steps.text: Pitch the taxi firm a fixed monthly maintenance price
Learn the taxi firm's AI maintenance booking system
Check vacancies at the bus company workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that one's scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for normal people and the government needs to slow it or pay people through it. I'd say that to Hassan and anyone at the station café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2028 the taxi firm's computer does all the planning, and probably finds a big automated garage. My hands are still needed until about 2031, but maybe not at Station Road. Then the robots come, and I'd be thirty-one with two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd cut everything, cancel the streaming and the gym, and get to a month of savings. I'd apply at the bus workshop properly, because a public bus company might move slower. In the first year after it arrives, I'd look for anything with a long contract, even if it pays less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like hearing the brakes go soft halfway down a hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena we're not buying a car or going on holiday this year, and that it's not forever. She'd be worried about her supermarket job too, with all the self-checkouts. We'd make a list of what we can cut together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three years of wages, but I'd spend them knowing it's coming. Maybe it gives me time to get into the bus company. I'd rather be inside a big employer when the robots show up than in a small garage.

say: It's **too fast** for normal people with normal bills to keep up.
Government must **slow it** or pay people through it.
think: By **2028** the taxi firm's computer may move its cars elsewhere.
I'd be **thirty-one** with two weeks of savings once robots come.
do: **Cut everything** and build to a month of savings.
Look for work with a **long contract** in the first year.
feel: **Alarmed**, like brakes going soft on a hill.
S2.quote: I'd rather be inside a big employer when the robots show up than in a small garage.
fieldNote: Ivan uses the **three-year gap** to get into a bigger, slower employer.
His household risk is double: **Lena's** supermarket job is also exposed.
He's pragmatic, wanting **long contracts** over pay.

steps.text: Cancel streaming and the gym this month
Build savings up to one month of expenses
Apply for a mechanic job at the bus company workshop
Ask local politicians to fund wage support during the change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more manageable. You'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready but don't panic. Five years is enough for a sensible person to make a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, 2031 is when the thinking side goes, so booking and fault-finding. 2034 for the robots. I'd be thirty-four. If I'm at the bus workshop by then, I've got a chance of staying on to look after the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply at the bus company this year or next. I'd do a short course on electric buses and high-voltage safety, since the bus company is going electric. I'd keep saving twenty-five a week and up it if I get the bus job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be doing something about it, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Hassan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel bad, but yes, if the bus job came up. Hassan would understand, he's a businessman. I'd give him proper notice and help train whoever replaced me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the bus job mean for you and Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bus job would mean better pay, a pension and fixed shifts. Maybe we could finally save a bit and think about a deposit. That would change a lot.

say: Get ready but **don't panic**, because there's time to think it through.
Five years is enough for a sensible person to **make a plan**.
think: Booking and **fault-finding** go in 2031, robots come in 2034.
Being at the **bus workshop** by then gives me a chance.
do: Apply at the **bus company** this year or next.
Take a short **electric bus** and high-voltage safety course.
Keep saving **twenty-five a week**, more with a bus job.
S3.quote: A bus job would mean better pay, a pension and fixed shifts.
fieldNote: Five years gives Ivan time to move to a **bigger employer**.
He'd leave Hassan with **proper notice** and help train a replacement.
The bus job could open the way to a **deposit** for him and Lena.

steps.text: Apply for a bus workshop job within two years
Take a high-voltage safety course for electric buses
Save twenty-five a week, raising it with a bus job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. I'd be thirty-seven before the thinking stuff all goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time to sort this out properly, so governments have no excuse. I'd tell young lads to learn electrics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I've got a normal decade first. I'd stay at Station Road for a while, then try the bus company. The robots in 2039 are a long way away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep saving, and get the high-voltage course done within three years. I'd watch what other mechanics do and copy what works. Lena and I would plan a holiday at last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more about the money than the AI. Ten years of low pay is still ten years of low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for to know when to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the taxi firm starts using an AI system to book us, that's my first sign. If other small garages start closing, that's the second. Then I'd move to the bus company before it gets crowded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena and I would probably try for kids around thirty. With two years, no way. With ten, I think we could.

say: There's **plenty of time** to sort this out, so governments have no excuse.
think: I've got a **normal decade** before the big change.
Robots in **2039** are a long way off for me.
do: Get the **high-voltage course** done within three years.
Watch what **other mechanics** do and copy what works.
Plan a **holiday** with Lena at last.
S4.quote: Ten years of low pay is still ten years of low pay.
fieldNote: Ivan has clear **warning signs**: the taxi firm's booking AI, small garages closing.
Low pay keeps him **uneasy** even with a decade.
Time makes **children around thirty** feel possible.

steps.text: Keep working at Station Road Motors for now
Finish a high-voltage course within three years
Watch for the taxi firm's AI booking before moving jobs
Plan to try for children with Lena around thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the taxi firm's computer could move our work before I've even got a back-up. What would help is a fair, fast way into bigger employers like the bus company, and some wage support if the garage shuts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the drivers. The taxi drivers are on even thinner money than me. When people talk about AI, they forget that small people like us depend on each other: the taxi drivers on me, and me on the taxi drivers.

headlineQuote: Small people like us depend on each other: the taxi drivers on me, and me on the taxi drivers.
portrait: Ivan, 27, services a **taxi fleet** and walk-ins at a garage behind the train station.
He has **two weeks** of savings and lives with Lena, who works at a supermarket.
He's pragmatic and **steady**, using AI only to write quotes.
His key risk is the **taxi contract** going to a bigger garage if AI shops on price.
With any warning he'd aim for the **bus company**, for a pension and fixed shifts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, if the taxi firm's computer moves its work before he has a back-up.
whatWouldHelp: A fair route into **bigger employers** like the bus company.
